analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card inactivity fees and requires card issuers' annual fees to be reasonable.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote in the House and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act, following the Credit CARD Act of 2009, to bar credit card companies from charging fees because a customer did not use the card, did not carry a balance, or did not borrow a minimum amount. It would let a customer cancel a card within 45 days if the issuer added an annual fee that was not there when the account was opened, without the cancellation hurting the customer's credit score. It would also require any annual fee to be reasonable, with the Federal Reserve writing rules to define that within six months. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary credit card holders. People who keep a card for emergencies but rarely use it would no longer be charged for that choice, since the bill bans fees tied to failing to use the card, failing to carry a balance, or failing to borrow a minimum amount. Anyone whose card issuer adds a new annual fee could cancel within 45 days without that cancellation lowering their credit score, and any annual fee charged would have to meet a 'reasonable' standard the Federal Reserve would define in rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders who pay fees

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits creditors from imposing any fee related to a consumer's failure to use the card, carry a balance, or obtain a minimum amount of credit [S3].

Allows a consumer to cancel within 45 days of notice of a newly imposed annual fee, pay off the balance on the old terms, and bars the creditor from taking action that would hurt the consumer's ability to get credit because of that cancellation [S3].
Requires annual fees to be reasonable and directs the Federal Reserve to issue final rules within six months establishing standards for assessing whether an annual fee is reasonable [S3].
Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so a credit score may not be lowered because a consumer cancelled a card account in accordance with the bill's cancellation provision [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers. Fees charged to people who do not use their cards or do not carry balances would be banned, new annual fees could trigger cancellations that cannot count against the customer's credit score, and annual fees would be subject to a Federal Reserve 'reasonableness' standard. Issuers might respond by tightening who qualifies for cards or raising rates for those who do.

drawbacks.text: Restricting how issuers can charge non-users and capping annual fees could make issuers less willing to offer cards to people with weaker credit, since those customers would be harder to make profitable [S3].
The 'reasonable annual fee' standard would leave the actual limits to Federal Reserve rulemaking, so the practical protection would depend entirely on how strictly the Fed wrote its rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits to card holders are clear: fees for not using a card are hard to defend, and the credit-score protection makes the cancellation right real rather than theoretical. The main cost is that issuers could restrict access to credit or raise rates to make up fee revenue, and the vagueness of the 'reasonable' standard means much would ride on Fed rules. On balance the protections outweigh those risks for the households the fees hit hardest, though the bill alone would not have solved fee creep.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Betty Sutton introduced the bill on October 29, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
The bill had 15 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, who kept the ability to charge inactivity-type fees and set annual fees without a 'reasonableness' standard. Consumers who rarely use their cards kept bearing the risk of those fees, though many of the same practices were later addressed through the Credit CARD Act of 2009's implementing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers kept fee flexibility

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call exists; support was entirely from one party.

industries.note: The bill bans fees for not using a card or not carrying a balance, lets customers cancel penalty-free when a new annual fee appears, and subjects annual fees to a Fed reasonableness standard. Issuers profit from exactly these fees, charged largely to people who use cards lightly or carry no debt.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and score developers
industries.note: The bill bars lowering a consumer's credit score because of a cancellation made under the bill, limiting how score developers can factor account cancellations. The practical effect for consumers is small but direct.
